extracted.intended_audience: model aeroplane builders and experimenters (hobbyists and early aviation experimenters)
extracted.subtask_short: model aeroplane motor and propeller design
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for selecting, constructing, and tuning motors and propellers for model aeroplanes, with numerical examples and design methods. Aimed at hobbyist experimenters building rubber-, spring-, compressed-air-, steam-, petrol- or electrically-driven models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motor energy-density comparison (rubber vs steel springs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubber has a much greater superiority over steel or other springs, because in stretch-twisted rubber far more energy can be stored up weight for weight. One pound weight of elastic can be made to store up some 320 ft.-lb. of energy, and steel only some 65 lb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer rubber motors for model flyers because of much higher energy per weight. Use steel or flat springs only for experimental studies of weight distribution or balance where rubber is unsuitable. Note that gearing for steel springs adds weight and friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiral steel-spring motor as a secondary option
rubrics_metrics.description: A more efficient form of spring motor, doing away with gearing troubles, is to use a long spiral spring (as long as the rubber strands) made of medium-sized piano wire, similar in principle to those used in some roller-blinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although experimented with, such spiral steel springs still do not compare with rubber for energy density, but are the best among steel-spring options and avoid complex gearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compressed-air motor practicality and weight penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Compressed-air motors appear ideal on paper but in practice reservoir and cylinder weights, plus required pressures, make them heavy and short-lived for model aeroplanes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example numbers: pneumatic drill works ~80 lb. pressure and uses ~55 cu. ft. free air/min per horsepower. A 3 ft × 1½ in reservoir of light metal likely weighs ≥4 oz; at 80 lb. pressure would give only ~10–30 seconds flight. Expect the entire compressed-air motor plant to weigh at least one-third of the aeroplane (on small scales possibly one-half), making it generally impractical compared with rubber or steam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compressed-air working-pressure and heating trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Using reducing valves or heating the air alters efficiency: heating before admission increases volume and reduces consumption, but adds fuel and burner weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working scheme: use reducing valve to maintain constant working pressure (e.g., 90–150 lb), or heat air (e.g., to ~320°F) to increase volume by ~50% and reduce consumption accordingly. Balance weight of fuel/burner against gains; aim to work motor at as low a pressure as practicable to avoid dead unused air as the reservoir pressure falls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steam-driven motor viability and boiler is the critical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Steam engines have been used successfully (e.g., Langley) but the principal difficulty is making a boiler of almost no weight which will give sufficient steam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Langley example: engine ~1–1½ H.P., moving parts 26 oz; boiler ~5 lb (continuous helix copper tubing), total aeroplane ~30 lb, flight ~1½ minutes. Expect engine to work out at ≈7 lb per H.P. Use flash-type boilers of copper or steel tubing (copper for safety) and working pressures of 150–200 lb/sq.in. Boiler design consumes much time; be prepared for high technical skill and trial-and-error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steam engine fuel/boiler weight-economy trick
rubrics_metrics.description: Use spirit (methylated spirit) as both fuel and boiler working fluid and cause exhaust to eject onto the burning spirit, so exhaust aids combustion and saves weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using volatile hydrocarbons reduces required vaporization temperature and can economize without adding condenser weight. Consider safety and rapid fuel consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turbine engines require small-diameter, low-pitch propellers
rubrics_metrics.description: When experimenting with an engine of the turbine type we must use a propeller of small diameter and pitch, owing to the very high velocity at which such engines run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turbines run at very high RPM; choose propeller geometry suited to high tip speeds and consider matching to turbine power/shaft speed. Turbine solutions are expert-level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale effects: smaller models are disproportionately harder
rubrics_metrics.description: The smaller the model the more difficult the problem--halve your aeroplane, and your difficulties increase anything from fourfold to tenfold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect nonlinear scaling penalties in power, weight, and heat losses; avoid over-optimism when shrinking full-size designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petrol (gasoline) motor feasibility with size/weight caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Petrol motors appear to be a potential solution and have been used; few petrol-driven model aeroplanes have actually flown. Example: Mr. Stanger's four-cylinder engine weighed 5½ lb and developed 1¼ H.P. at 1300 rpm; total machine ~21 lb and rose at ~16 mph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petrol engines can be practical but require careful design for weight, carburetion, ignition, and cooling. Copy proven full-sized arrangements when possible. Include an automatic shut-off (e.g., clockwork) if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-cylinder petrol engines discouraged for models
rubrics_metrics.description: No success has as yet attended the use of a single-cylinder petrol motor on a model aeroplane; vibration is excessive, heavier in proportion, and less efficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multi-cylinder arrangements to reduce vibration; if attempting single-cylinder, plan for vibration management and accept lower efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric motors impractical for free-flight models
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to use electric motors for model aeroplanes. They are altogether too heavy, apart even from the accumulator or source of electric energy, for the power derivable from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a 2-oz motor giving static thrust of 3 oz would need an accumulator of ~4½ oz (without casing), requiring multiple units and short run-times of 10–15 seconds. For actual flight, electric systems are usually too heavy; may be used for scale non-flying models or demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propeller position: tractor (front) vs propulsive (rear)
rubrics_metrics.description: In model aeroplanes the propeller is usually situated either in front (tractor) or in the rear (propulsive). For models, propulsive screws (pusher) are much the best owing to ease of launching and ability to land without damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider constructional factors and similarity to full-sized successful designs (copy for petrol-driven models). Never place propeller in centre or where it shortens elastic motor strands; that will harm flight quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of blades: minimum two, two preferred for aerial models
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretically one blade would be sufficient but balance is primary; minimum number of blades is therefore two. In aerial models two blades are practically invariable; marine models sometimes use three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose two blades for ease of construction and lower weight. Increasing blade count increases weight and can reduce efficiency for models; only increase blades when balance or other constraints demand it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan versus propeller distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A fan (ventilating) and a propeller are not the same: a fan moves small quantity of air at high velocity (often while stationary), whereas a propeller should move a large quantity of air at small velocity to create thrust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid designing a propeller like a fan (many blades, narrow disk intent). For thrust efficiency favor designs that accelerate a large mass of air slowly rather than a small mass quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch and slip: definitions and desirable slip ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitch is the linear distance a screw would move in one revolution in a solid medium; slip is the distance lost because the propeller does not actually advance that full distance in a yielding fluid. For aerial propellers a slip of ~25% is quite good, 40% bad; possibly about 15% may be best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use slip to assess propulsive efficiency: Speed (ft/min) = pitch (ft) × RPM − slip (ft/min). Some slip is necessary to produce thrust. Target moderate slip (10–25%), avoid very high slip (~40%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch coefficient / pitch ratio guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitch ratio = pitch divided by diameter. Mean full-sized machine pitch ratio ~0.62 (range 0.4–1.2); Wright machine probably ~1. Rubber-driven model propellers often use much higher pitch ratios, sometimes >3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher pitch ratio (within limits) tends to better efficiency and allows slower RPM; for rubber motors avoid too fine a pitch which makes the propeller 'race' and increases slip. Writer preference: pitch ratio ≈1.5 for rubber-driven models; T.W.K. Clarke recommends tip pitch angle ≤45° and pitch ratio ~3.14 as one recommendation. Balance pitch ratio against diameter and motor characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diameter relative to wing span
rubrics_metrics.description: Diameter recommendations vary: Clarke says diameter should be one-quarter the span of the machine; the writer prefers a larger diameter (one-third to one-half the span) and not less than one-third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasing diameter decreases pitch ratio for a given pitch; writer prefers lower pitch ratio and increased diameter for improved performance. Do not use diameters smaller than about one-third span for rubber-driven models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform theoretical pitch along blade
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretically the pitch (from boss to tip) should at all points be the same; the angle decreases as one approaches the tips so that all parts advance the same distance per revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design blades with decreasing angle from hub to tip to achieve uniform pitch. If pitch is non-uniform some portions will drag and others will overwork the air, reducing efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hollow-faced, streamlined blade sections
rubrics_metrics.description: A propeller is a particular form of aeroplane and should therefore be hollow faced and partake of the 'stream line' form. A flat-faced blade cuts into the air with considerable shock and is inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use curved/hollow-faced blades to reduce shock and improve mean effective pitch; curved face causes increasing pitch from cutting to trailing edge — interpret pitch as mean effective pitch in that case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blade area and width: narrow blades preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: For aerial propellers narrow blades are best. Thrust depends more on disk area than blade width; multiplicity of blades and large blade area tend to inefficiency, apart from weight and construction difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make blades as narrow as practical consistent with required strength and stiffness. Avoid excessive blade area; separate blades sufficiently so one does not disturb air for the next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended rotational speeds (RPM) limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A higher speed than 900 r.p.m. does not appear desirable; even 700 or less is generally preferable. For twin-screw propellers with tip angles 40–45°, as low a velocity as 500 or even less would be better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design propeller pitch and diameter to achieve desired thrust at conservative RPMs (≤900 rpm, preferably ≤700; twin-screw even lower). High RPMs increase inefficiencies and stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: No benefit from shrouding or rings around tips
rubrics_metrics.description: No improvement whatever is obtained by the use of any kind of shrouding or ring round the propeller tips, or by corrugating the surface, or using cylindrical/cone-shaped chambers; allow free air-feed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not invest in tip rings, shrouds, or corrugation expecting efficiency gains for small model propellers; well-designed propellers draw air inward and do not 'throw' it off centrifugally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propeller should act on a tube of air, not a cylinder
rubrics_metrics.description: The propeller should be so constructed as to act upon a tube and not a 'cylinder' of air. Central cut-away cylinder-type propellers waste central area and add resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid designs that rely on a central disk or cylinder of air; maximize effective disk/tube action and avoid central cutaways that add drag without propulsive benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended blade shape and thickness taper
rubrics_metrics.description: A good shape for the blades is rectangular with rounded corners; the width near the boss should be about one-half the width at the tip. The thickness should diminish uniformly from boss to tip. The pitch should be uniform and large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round corners with radius ≈ one-quarter of blade width. Keep thickness minimal consistent with required strength. For wooden blades two-blade rectangular-with-rounded-corners shape is easy to make and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two hollow-faced blades geometry specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Two blades, hollow faced — maximum concavity one-third the distance from entering to trailing edge; ratio AT:OP (width) ≈ 0.048 (1:21). Convex surface is as important as concave. If entering/trailing edges have curvature rules apply: straight edge should be trailing if paired with curved, and concave edge trailing if both curved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow proportions for concavity and width-to-depth ratio to mirror aerofoil analogy. Ensure the convex surface is streamlined; observe edge-curvature rules to set correct entering/trailing orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical propeller design/drawing method
rubrics_metrics.description: Method to design a propeller by scale drawing: choose diameter and pitch, draw centreline and half-pitch, describe semicircle for radius, divide semicircle and parallelogram into equal parts, draw lines and trace tip path to get tip path and tip angle. Example: diameter 14 in, pitch 52 in gives tip angle ≈44° and blade area calculation shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the described geometric construction (divide semicircle into e.g., 12 parts) to derive blade tip path and angles, and proportion blade breadth (e.g., tip breadth twice boss breadth). Calculate swept disk area (π/4 × diameter²) and blade area for loading estimates. This provides a practical way to translate theoretical pitch/diameter choices into a manufacturable blade outline.
